body.heading: Build the gauge
paragraphs: Your adult cuts the top off a clear plastic bottle. Put small stones in the bottom so the wind cannot tip it over, then turn the cut top upside down into the bottle like a funnel.
Pour in water up to the stones and mark that line as zero with the marker. Your adult can help you mark centimetre lines up the side with a ruler.

body.heading: Catch the rain
paragraphs: Stand your gauge outside on flat ground, away from trees and roofs. After it rains, look at the water level. How many centimetres of rain fell?
Rain gauges help farmers, gardeners, and weather watchers. Yours is a real science tool, even though it is made from an old bottle.

body.heading: Keep a rain diary
paragraphs: Empty the gauge after each rainy day and write the number in your notebook. Add a drawing of the day's sky.
After a few weeks, add up all your rain. Which week was the wettest? Your diary holds the story of your weather.

takeaway: A bottle, a ruler, and a marker make a real rain gauge that measures how much rain falls.
materials: A clear plastic bottle (an adult cuts it)
safetyNotes: An adult must do all the cutting — plastic edges can be sharp. Children should never use the knife for this job.
screenFreeExtension: Measure other water at home — how much water is in your cup, your bath, or a watering can.
